newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Switzerland, Russia to sign debt restructure deal.
newsitem.headline: Switzerland, Russia to sign debt restructure deal.

text.p: Switzerland and Russia will sign on Thursday a debt-restructuring deal involving debt of 385 million Swiss francs ($271 million), Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday.

Chernomyrdin told leading Swiss business people the debt restructuring, done under the framework of the Paris Club of official debtors, had been agreed by the two countries and would be signed when he visits the Swiss capital of Berne.

Chernomyrdin, on his first official visit to Switzerland, will on Thursday meet Swiss president Arnold Koller and Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti to discuss bilateral issues, developments in Russia and European security.
Chernomyrdin, who arrived in Switzerland on Wednesday, also said talks on unguaranteed commercial debts owed to Switzerland from Russia would continue.
"In this connection I want to underscore Russia's principled position. We will repay all our debt, without exceptions," Chernomyrdin said.
Russian banks were also interested in strengthening their presence in Switzerland and cooperation with Swiss banks.
Some of Russia's "largest and most solid banks" were also interested in getting Swiss banking licences, Chernomyrdin said, asking the business people for their support in these efforts.
Switzerland is the second largest foreign investor in Russia with investments of $1.351 billion last year, Chernomyrdin said, noting that Switzerland was among its top 10 trading partners.
He noted with satisfaction that 50 percent of that amount came from direct investments from such companies as electrical engineering group ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG and food and beverage group Nestle.

In 1996 foreigners invested some $6 billion in Russia, three times the amount in 1995, and Chernomyrdin said he hoped to increase this to $20 billion annually by the year 2000 as the economy improves and the reform programmes continue.
Chernomyrdin said his aim for 1997 was to reduce annual average inflation to 12 percent, down from 21 percent in 1996.
He noted that Switzerland had never adopted a discriminatory attitude in its dealings with Russia, in contrast with many other countries, including some European.
Chernomyrdin also said he wanted extend bilateral ties to Switzerland and said he believed there was a potential to expand relations between the two countries.
After his trip to Berne, Chernomyrdin heads to the Swiss resort of Davos to attend the World Economic Forum, which runs from January 30 to February 4.
